nodes.label: River instruments: stories from the navigation hall, English · river collection · 284 MB, Wi-Fi required, Hide chapters, A river pilots desk, Start at the pilots desk and examine the folded river chart beneath its glass cover. The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Get audio, End of observed component

nodes.label: River instruments: stories from the navigation hall, English · river collection · 284 MB, Wi-Fi required, Hide chapters, A river pilots desk, Start at the pilots desk and examine the folded river chart beneath its glass cover. The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Get audio, End of observed component

nodes.label: River instruments: stories from the navigation hall, English · river collection · 284 MB, Ready to download, Hide chapters, A river pilots desk, Start at the pilots desk and examine the folded river chart beneath its glass cover. The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Get audio, End of observed component

The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Get audio

The opening voice explains how crews planned a passage around shifting sandbanks and why a familiar route still needed careful attention on every journey., Measuring the current, Beside the current meter, listen to a surveyor describe taking a reading from a small boat. The account connects the instrument to a practical decision about when to leave the landing, without asking you to perform a calculation yourself., The bridge watch, At the bridge model, follow the lookout route from one side of the deck to the other. A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date. This chapter explains how observations about weather, repairs, and waiting at a landing could help the next crew prepare for the same stretch of river., Repairing a navigation lamp, The lamp bench shows the small parts a keeper carried when a light failed. The narrator follows one routine repair and describes checking the beam from the water, where an apparently bright lamp might still be difficult to recognize., Voices at the crossing, Listen near the ferry photograph to hear three short memories of the crossing. Each speaker describes a different task, and the pauses between their accounts leave time to compare the landing shown in the image with the route map., Reading the river today, End beside the modern river map and find the old crossing on its edge. The closing chapter describes which habits of observation remain useful, even when the crew also carries electronic charts and receives regular messages from the shore station., Wi-Fi only, Requested, End of observed component

A retired crew member recalls watching for a low marker while another person kept track of the approaching bend in the river., Soundings in shallow water, The sounding line display introduces a job that required patience and clear spoken signals. Listen while looking at the marked lengths on the rope, then compare the working line with the later mechanical instrument in the neighboring case., Keeping a voyage log, Pause at the open logbook and notice the short entries written beside each date.
